content: Algorithms, as defined by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) in 2006, do not qualify as processes and are therefore not patentable. This principle was established in the case of Gottschalk v. Benson. However, practical applications of algorithms can sometimes be patented. For instance, in the case of Diamond v. Diehr, the use of a simple feedback algorithm to improve the curing process of synthetic rubber was deemed patentable. The patenting of software, particularly algorithms, remains a contentious issue, with significant criticism directed at patents involving data compression algorithms, such as the LZW patent held by Unisys. Additionally, certain cryptographic algorithms are subject to export restrictions, as outlined in regulations governing the export of cryptography. The term algorithm originates from the name of the 9th-century Persian mathematician Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi. His works introduced Indian numerals and algebraic concepts to the broader world. Al-Khwarizmi worked in Baghdad during its era as a hub of scientific study and trade. Initially, the term algorism referred specifically to the rules for performing arithmetic using Arabic numerals. Over time, through European Latin translations of al-Khwarizmi's name, the term evolved into algorithm by the 18th century. The word eventually came to encompass all definitive procedures for solving problems or performing tasks. In ancient times, tally marks were used to keep track of quantities such as livestock, grain, or money. This involved accumulating stones, scratching marks on sticks, or creating discrete symbols in clay. Tally marks prominently feature in unary numeral system arithmetic, which is used in Turing machine computations and their post-Turing developments. The manipulation of symbols as placeholders for numbers, a concept central to algebra, has its roots in the work of ancient Greek geometers, Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi (often regarded as the father of algebra), and Western European mathematicians. This culminated in Leibniz's concept of the calculus ratiocinator around 1680. The invention of mechanical devices with discrete states played a pivotal role in the development of computational systems. The weight-driven clock, particularly the verge escapement mechanism, is credited as a key invention that introduced the tick-tock of mechanical clocks. The Jacquard loom (1801), a precursor to Hollerith punch cards (1887), and telephone switching technologies laid the groundwork for the development of early computers. By the mid-1800s, the telegraph, a precursor to the telephone, was widely used, employing discrete encoding of letters as dots and dashes. This was followed by the Teletype (circa 1910), which utilized punched paper and Baudot code. Electromechanical relay-based telephone-switching networks, invented in 1835, influenced the work of George Stibitz, who developed a binary adding device in 1937 while working at Bell Laboratories. Stibitz's invention addressed the inefficiencies of mechanical calculators with gears. The mathematics of the 19th and early 20th centuries saw significant advancements in symbolic manipulation and formal systems. George Boole (1847, 1854), Gottlob Frege (1879), and Giuseppe Peano (1888–1889) reduced arithmetic to sequences of symbols governed by rules. Peano's The Principles of Arithmetic (1888) was the first attempt at axiomatizing mathematics in a symbolic language. Frege's work was later expanded upon by Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell in their Principia Mathematica (1910–1913). During this period, several paradoxes emerged, such as the Burali-Forti paradox (1897), Russell's paradox (1902–03), and the Richard paradox (1906). These paradoxes prompted Kurt Gödel's groundbreaking 1931 paper, which addressed the limits of formal systems and recursion. Gödel's work, influenced by Jacques Herbrand, led to the development of general recursion theory, further refined by Stephen Kleene in the 1930s and 1940s. Alonzo Church's 1936 proof demonstrated the unsolvability of the Entscheidungsproblem (decision problem). Emil Post's definition of effective calculability described a process in which a worker mindlessly follows a list of instructions to manipulate symbols. Alan Turing's 1936–1937 proof of the unsolvability of the Entscheidungsproblem introduced the concept of the a-machine (Turing machine), which closely resembled Post's formulation. J. Barkley Rosser defined effective method in terms of a machine in 1939. Kleene later proposed a precursor to Church's Thesis, which he called Thesis I in 1943, and subsequently renamed it Church's Thesis in 1952, while also proposing Turing's Thesis. These developments laid the foundation for modern computational theory.
